# What This Document Addresses

Where M365, Azure, and AWS are boundaries the agency reaches through a cloud provider, VMware is the agency's own virtualization layer — the hypervisor, network-virtualization, and cluster-management estate the agency owns, racks, and patches directly. It carries the identical class of obligations the CSP books carry, at the virtualization plane instead of the provider plane: baseline configuration and settings (CM-2, CM-6), flaw remediation (SI-2), and vulnerability monitoring (RA-5). VMware's native stack *actuates* all three; the coordination role is to make each one owned, clocked, approved where it changes state, and evidenced. CM-2's registered closure sits in Vol III Book 03 (Patch & Systems Management); this book touches CM-2 only through vSphere Configuration Profiles' actuation of that baseline, so its *Authorities Closed Here* table registers the coordination closures CM-6, SI-2, and RA-5 — the identical registration pattern Vol VII Books 03 and 06 use for Azure and AWS.

This book runs the same five-step loop as Vol VII Books 02, 03, and 06 — **test → detect drift → raise a typed task against the reconciled CI → actuate on the native surface → close with evidence** — over the three VMware control engines. The loop is deliberately identical across surfaces: one coordination pattern, four platforms, so the evidence and the assessor-facing story are uniform regardless of whether the workload sits in a hyperscaler or on the agency's own racks.

# The VMware Control Engines and Their Coordination Role

| VMware engine | Owns (actuation) | Control | ServiceNow coordination role |
|---|---|---|---|
| **vSphere Configuration Profiles** | Host/cluster desired-state configuration compliance and drift remediation | CM-2, CM-6 | Non-compliant host/cluster → Change/remediation task against the CI; track native remediation to closure |
| **VCF Operations + NSX Distributed Firewall** | Continuous compliance/benchmark posture across the VCF fleet; segmentation-policy (DFW) drift and rule hygiene | CM-6, RA-5 | Violation/finding → prioritized Vulnerability-Response task; SLA by exposure |
| **vSphere Lifecycle Manager (vLCM)** | ESXi image/patch compliance assessment and remediation | SI-2, SI-2(2/3) | Non-compliant image state → Change/Incident; SLA-class task keyed to KEV/exposure |

::: {.aan-note}
**This volume governs the virtualization layer, by doctrine — not the guest OS, firmware, or physical hardware.** vSphere Configuration Profiles, VCF Operations, NSX Distributed Firewall, and vLCM operate ESXi, vCenter, and NSX — the hypervisor and network-virtualization control plane. They do not patch the operating system running *inside* a VMware-hosted VM (that guest OS reconciles through its own native stack, Vol III Book 03, on the identical SI-2 discipline this book uses for the hypervisor), and they do not manage server firmware or physical hardware lifecycle (a separate, vendor-specific management-plane surface, Management-Plane Coordination Doctrine, Vol 0 Book 00). **This volume coordinates the ESXi/vCenter/NSX virtualization surface only.** OCI reconciles into the same ServiceNow SI-2 queue in a later follow-up (its native stack is catalogued in Vol III Book 03); ServiceNow already coordinates a single queue, so adding that surface later needs no rework here.
:::

# Control Engine 1 — vSphere Configuration Profiles (CM-2 / CM-6)

vSphere Configuration Profiles is the current desired-state configuration mechanism for ESXi hosts and clusters, superseding the older Host Profiles model. It checks hosts against a declared cluster-level desired configuration, reports drift, and can remediate a subset natively. The coordination role covers the rest — and the change control around all of it.

- **Test:** cluster/host compliance state is read against the desired configuration (compliant / non-compliant, with the specific setting that drifted).
- **Detect + Raise:** a non-compliant host or cluster becomes a ServiceNow **Change** (for a controlled configuration change) tagged with the drifted setting, the mapped control (CM-2/CM-6), severity, and the reconciled host/cluster CI. An *exemption* is not silent — it is a request with an approver and an expiry, so a configuration exception is reviewable (the same discipline as an M365 CA exception, an Azure Policy exemption, and an AWS Config exemption).
- **Actuate:** vSphere Configuration Profiles remediation runs against the cluster (a pre-check confirms hosts can enter maintenance mode and DRS can evacuate VMs where needed), or the owning team applies the configuration through infrastructure-as-code (Vol VI Book 01/06). ServiceNow does not write the host configuration.
- **Close:** the next compliance check flips the host/cluster to compliant; ServiceNow closes and stamps the evidence.

# Control Engine 2 — VCF Operations + NSX Distributed Firewall (CM-6 / RA-5)

VCF Operations is the VMware Cloud Foundation posture engine within the GCC Moderate boundary; Vol III Book 04 owns the posture architecture and Vol III Book 02 owns the assessment doctrine. It continuously monitors the VCF fleet against industry benchmarks and custom policies, surfaces violations and risk areas, and — through the VMware Advanced Cyber Compliance service — layers continuous compliance enforcement on top of that visibility. NSX Distributed Firewall (DFW) is the micro-segmentation policy engine for east-west traffic between workloads; its rule state and rule hygiene (including stale/inactive rules) are visible through the same VCF Operations for Networks telemetry this engine consumes. (VCF Operations' broader AIOps/capacity-management capabilities are a later follow-up, out of scope here.) The coordination role turns both engines' findings into prioritized, owned remediation work.

- **Test + Detect:** VCF Operations compliance-benchmark violations (misconfiguration against a declared standard) and NSX DFW policy/rule-hygiene findings (segmentation drift, stale rules) are read via the respective management APIs.
- **Raise:** each finding becomes a ServiceNow **Vulnerability Response** task against the reconciled CI, with a severity and an SLA class derived from exposure and KEV status — the risk-based prioritization CISA BOD 22-01 and the PAIN-rating model (BOD 26-04; FedRAMP VDR-TFR-PVR) call for, detailed under Control Engine 3 below.
- **Actuate:** the owning team remediates on the native surface — a configuration fix, an NSX DFW rule correction, or a patch (vSphere Lifecycle Manager, below).
- **Close:** the finding clears on the next VCF Operations assessment; ServiceNow closes the task, and the mean-time-to-remediate becomes an SI-2(3) / KSI metric.

# Control Engine 3 — vSphere Lifecycle Manager / vLCM (SI-2)

vSphere Lifecycle Manager assesses and remediates ESXi host image and patch compliance across the cluster. It is the SI-2 actuation engine for the hypervisor; the coordination role reconciles its results into change/incident work with the SLA discipline SI-2(3) requires.

- **Test:** vLCM reports each host's image/patch compliance against the cluster's desired image (compliant / non-compliant, with the specific component that drifted).
- **Raise:** a non-compliant host becomes a ServiceNow **Change** (scheduled maintenance window) or **Incident** (an out-of-cycle KEV exposure), with an SLA class keyed to KEV/exposure — the PAIN-rating model (BOD 26-04; FedRAMP VDR-TFR-PVR), detailed below. The same SLA discipline is what the OCI patch queue will reconcile into when it is added later (Vol III Book 03).
- **Actuate:** vLCM remediates the host in the approved maintenance window — evacuating VMs via DRS, entering maintenance mode, applying the desired image, and exiting maintenance mode; ServiceNow does not push the image, it schedules and governs it.
- **Close + evidence:** the post-remediation compliance check confirms the host matches the desired image; the Change record, approval, window, and re-check become the SI-2(2) machine-readable remediation-status evidence.

::: {.aan-note}
**"SLA by exposure" has a name and a published table — the Potential Agency Impact (PAIN) rating.** FedRAMP's Vulnerability Detection and Response ruleset (VDR-TFR-PVR) sets mitigation/remediation timeframes by PAIN rating crossed with exploitability and internet-reachability:

| PAIN rating | Likely-exploitable, internet-reachable | Likely-exploitable, not internet-reachable | Not likely exploitable |
|---|---|---|---|
| PAIN-5 | 4 days | 8 days | 32 days |
| PAIN-4 | 8 days | 32 days | 64 days |
| PAIN-3 | 32 days | 64 days | 192 days |
| PAIN-2 | 96 days | 160 days | 192 days |

A CISA-catalogued KEV must be remediated by the KEV catalog's own due date regardless of PAIN rating (VDR-TFR-KEV), even after full mitigation. These are the actual numbers a ServiceNow SLA-class task should encode — "SLA by exposure" is this table, not a general-purpose severity field.
:::

::: {.aan-caution}
**Baseline-based patching is being retired — this book targets vLCM Images.** VMware deprecated baseline-based patching starting with vSphere 8.0, with full removal in a later major release; the desired-state Images model is the forward path and the one this coordination pattern targets. An estate still running baseline-managed clusters reconciles through the same ServiceNow SI-2 queue, but the reconcile-exception queue should track the Images migration itself as a tracked closure item, not treat baseline mode as a permanent parallel path.
:::

# Continuous Monitoring Roll-Up (CA-7)

Each engine's loop emits its result into the continuous-monitoring feed: Configuration Profiles compliance percentage, open VCF Operations/NSX DFW findings by severity and age, vLCM image-compliance conformance. ServiceNow rolls these into a per-control VMware posture that Vol VII Book 04 turns into attestation and KSI evidence, keyed to the same reconciled asset identity the M365, Azure, and AWS postures use — so all four platforms produce *one* compliance picture, not four.

# Closure Necessity

::: {.aan-tip}
## Closure Necessity — VMware actuates; the estate still needs an owner and a clock
vSphere Configuration Profiles remediates, VCF Operations and NSX DFW surface, vLCM patches — the native stack is genuinely sufficient to *change state*, on the agency's own hardware exactly as it is on a hyperscaler's. What it does not supply is the governance wrapper: who owns this finding, by when, under whose approval, with what evidence. Strip the coordination layer and vCenter's own console shows green while the authorization package has no owned-and-evidenced record an assessor can trace. CM-6, SI-2, and RA-5 are closed by VMware; they are *operated* — owned, clocked, evidenced — here.
:::

# Honest Limits

- A task closes when the native re-evaluation passes; Configuration Profiles/VCF Operations assessment latency means "closed" can lag actual state by an evaluation cycle. Evidence timestamps record the cycle, not the instant.
- This book governs ESXi/vCenter/NSX only; guest-OS patching inside a VMware-hosted VM, physical-server firmware, and hardware lifecycle reconcile in from their own native stacks (Vol III Book 03). Treating this book as the whole management plane is a doctrine violation the reconcile-exception queue is meant to catch — the identical failure mode the Arc note in Vol VII Book 03 and the hybrid-activation note in Vol VII Book 06 guard against.
- Native vSphere Configuration Profiles remediation still carries a Change record — automated actuation does not waive change control (CM-3); it makes the change record's *actuator* the Configuration Profiles engine rather than a person.
- NSX Distributed Firewall's microsegmentation capability requires NSX Advanced edition or higher; an estate licensed below that tier does not have DFW policy state to reconcile, and that licensing gap belongs in the reconcile-exception queue rather than being silently absent from the posture roll-up.
- Baseline-managed clusters (the pre-vLCM-Images patching model) are on a deprecation path; see the caution under Control Engine 3.
